cultivar: Wuyi cai cha (local small-leaf population bushes)
processing: Fully oxidised, unsmoked Tongmu black made from a bud with one young leaf: withered, lightly rolled, oxidised and dried at low heat.
harvest_season: Spring, picked a few days after the Jin Jun Mei buds, from late April into May.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, slightly curved strands, mostly black and bronze with a scattering of gold tips.
appearance_wet: Tiny buds with one small copper leaf attached, very even.
taste_profile: Honey and longan like its bud-only sibling, with more body, a little more grip and a cocoa note from the leaf, and slightly less perfume.

brewing.notes: Same as Jin Jun Mei: gaiwan, water just under the boil, no rinse, short steeps. It is a little more forgiving of long steeps than the bud-only tea.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest; best within a year or two. Prices are a fraction of Jin Jun Mei and so is the fakery, but 'outside-mountain' lots are still common, so buy from a seller who names the village.
description:
Yin Jun Mei – 'silver' to Jin Jun Mei's 'gold' – is the second rung of the Tongmu bud-tea ladder that appeared in 2005–2006. Where Jin Jun Mei is the bud alone, Yin Jun Mei is a bud with one young leaf, picked a few days later from the same small-leaf bushes in the Wuyi nature reserve. It was launched alongside its famous sibling (there was briefly a 'copper' grade below it, now sold as Chi Gan) and it has quietly become the better buy.

The leaf is withered, lightly rolled, oxidised and dried without smoke, exactly like Jin Jun Mei; the only difference is the picking standard. One extra leaf changes the cup more than you would think: a little more tannin and cocoa, more body, slightly less of the honeyed perfume, and a dry leaf that is mostly black and bronze with fewer gold tips.

Expect honey and dried longan up front, cocoa and a gentle sweet-potato warmth underneath, a bit more grip than the bud tea and the same long, cool Tongmu finish. It runs eight to ten steeps in a gaiwan with water just under the boil, no rinse, and it tolerates a careless long steep better than Jin Jun Mei does. Western-style it makes a fine, bright pot at 3 g per 250 ml for two and a half minutes.

It is sold as the current spring harvest, usually in small foil packs, at perhaps a fifth to a tenth of the price of Jin Jun Mei from the same maker. The same caveat applies: the name is used on tea from far outside Tongmu, so buy from a seller who names the village and ask what the picking standard was. Uniformly golden, fluffy leaf is a sign of a different cultivar from a different province.

If you have ever paid for Jin Jun Mei and wondered what the fuss was, try a Yin Jun Mei from a named Tongmu maker first; it is the more honest introduction to the style.
sources_note: The former 'Tong Jun Mei' (copper) grade and its renaming to Chi Gan is reported by Tongmu makers; exact timeline uncertain.
